title: Gemini 4 Hydrogen: The Budget Model That Beat Google's Own Flagship
summary: Google's new Gemini 4 Hydrogen costs a fifth of a frontier model, runs 2.5x faster than the Flash it replaces, and still out-scores the pricier Gemini 4 Argon on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index.
content:
On November 12, Google shipped Gemini 4 Hydrogen, the model that replaces the Gemini 3.8 Flash line. It is not Google's most capable model. It may be the one most people end up using. Hydrogen is built for speed and cost — everyday coding, agentic workflows, and the AI Mode inside Google Search — and on the published numbers it does something awkward for Google: it out-scores the company's own flagship, Gemini 4 Argon, while costing a fraction of the price.

What shipped

The specs are unusually aggressive for a "workhorse" tier. Hydrogen costs $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens, with cache hits at $0.075. That is roughly a fifth of what a frontier-class model charges. It takes a one-million-token context window for input and can emit up to one million tokens of output, which matters for the long-document and video-summarization tasks Google is pushing it toward.

It also has four reasoning levels: low, medium, high (the default), and a new tier called xhigh. Argon offers only medium and high. The extra dial is the whole point — you pay for thinking only when a task needs it.

It is live everywhere at once: the Gemini API, AI Studio, Android Studio, the Gemini app, Google Search, and Google Antigravity for Pro and Ultra subscribers.

The benchmarks

Google's own framing is that Hydrogen beats the bigger Argon. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, that holds up.

Benchmark Hydrogen Carbon Argon
AA Intelligence Index 51 (54 at xhigh) 59 50
SWE-sweep (agentic coding) 13.5% 9.6% 4.3%
Agents' Last Exam v1.1 71.6% 77.4% 69.0%
OSWorld-2.1 (computer use) 77.6% 81.5% 74.7%

At its xhigh setting, Hydrogen reaches 54 — just behind Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol, which each hit 55 at their maximum effort. Argon trails at 50. On agent tasks, Google says Hydrogen takes first place on the Vals Tax Agent Bench (52.3%) and ties for first on the Vals Legal Research Bench (55.8%), and it ranks fifth overall on the Agent Arena leaderboard.

The jump that matters more

The headline is not Hydrogen beating Argon by a point. It is how far it moves past the model it replaces. Google says Hydrogen finishes tasks 2.5 times faster than Gemini 3.8 Flash at the default thinking level. On Terminal-Bench 4.1, the score jumps from 18.2% to 57%. Hallucinations fell by a factor of five, and the model recovers better when a tool call fails or a search comes back empty — the failure modes that quietly break agents in production.

Then there is the timing, which says a lot. Google announced its frontier model Carbon just two days earlier, and its own advice was to keep using Argon for daily coding work. Hydrogen makes that advice moot, and it leaves Argon looking obsolete less than four weeks after its release. That is not a roadmap; it is a fast-moving price-performance curve compressing two model tiers into one.

Takeaway

For a while, "cheap" meant "noticeably worse." Hydrogen is the clearest sign yet that the gap is closing from the bottom. It does not win on raw reasoning — Carbon and the top Claude and GPT models still lead there — but it gets close enough on most real tasks that paying frontier prices for them becomes hard to justify. If you run agents at any volume, the cost line is where this one bites. Google just reset the floor for what a mid-tier model should cost and do.

Sources: The Decoder, "Google's Gemini 4 Hydrogen outscores the bigger Argon just four weeks after its launch" (Nov 12, 2026); Google, "Introducing Gemini 4 Hydrogen" (Nov 12, 2026); Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index.
